\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Register Allocation Through Iterated Coalescing Revisited}
\author{D.~Ivanova and K.~Sato}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
Register allocation remains one of the most consequential phases of an
optimizing compiler: a poor allocation turns hot loops into sequences of
loads and stores, while a good one keeps values in registers across entire
loop nests. Since Chaitin's formulation of allocation as graph coloring,
and the coalescing refinements of Briggs and of George and Appel, the
problem has been considered largely solved for desktop targets. In this
paper we revisit iterated register coalescing in the context of deeply
pipelined embedded cores, where spill latency is dominated by a small,
multi-ported scratchpad rather than by cache.

\section{Background on Static Single Assignment Form}
A program is in static single assignment (SSA) form when every variable is
assigned at exactly one program point. Join points carry $\phi$-functions
that select among the definitions reaching them. SSA form simplifies
liveness analysis and makes the interference graph chordal, which in turn
permits coloring heuristics to behave predictably. Our allocator operates
on SSA directly and eliminates $\phi$-functions only after coloring.

\section{Register Allocation via Graph Coloring}
We follow the classic pipeline: build the interference graph, then iterate
simplify, coalesce, freeze, and potential-spill until the graph is empty
or an actual spill is forced. Coalescing removes copy instructions when
source and target do not interfere; iterated coalescing alternates
conservative coalescing with simplification so that copies removed early
do not prevent later coloring opportunities.

\section{Handling of Spill Code Placement}
When the graph cannot be colored with $k$ registers, a live range must be
spilled. We rank candidates by spill cost per unit of interference degree,
where cost is estimated from loop-nest depth and scratchpad access
latency. Short live ranges with cheap re-computation are rematerialized
instead of being stored.

\section{Experimental Evaluation on Embedded Benchmarks}
We implemented the allocator in a research backend and evaluated it on 28
programs from two embedded benchmark suites. Against a linear-scan
baseline, iterated coalescing reduces dynamic spill traffic by 41\% on
average and improves run time by 4.2\% on average, with the largest gains
on signal-processing kernels whose inner loops are register-bound.

\section{Related Work}
Chaitin introduced coloring-based allocation; Briggs added conservative
coalescing; George and Appel proposed iterated coalescing. Linear scan
remains the standard alternative for just-in-time and embedded compilers
where allocation time matters more than allocation quality.

\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
Iterated coalescing, long considered a desktop technique, pays off on
modern embedded cores when the spill cost model reflects scratchpad
latency. Future work includes a tighter integration of coalescing with
instruction scheduling and an empirical study of allocation-sensitive
vectorization.

\end{document}
